extracted.intended_audience: general public, scholars, historians of science, and readers interested in academic publishing
extracted.subtask_description: A popular-history article tracing the evolution and institutionalization of peer review/refereeing (especially at the Royal Society and later journals) and commenting on its purposes, limits, and adoption into modern scholarly practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of independent third-party expert referees
rubrics_metrics.description: With peer review, independent, third-party experts in the relevant field(s) assess manuscripts submitted to journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These expert peers referee the process particularly for technical matters beyond editors' knowledge; the referee principle is the core mechanism by which manuscripts are evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartial evaluation by specialists (close scrutiny)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review 'promises supposedly impartial evaluation of research, through close scrutiny by specialists.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This impartial close scrutiny is the justification for using peer review across journals, grant-making bodies, and government; the promise of impartiality is central to its perceived role in certifying quality and reliability of research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize inappropriate bias from social dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be 'inappropriate bias due to the social dynamics of the process.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges that different peer-review types may introduce more or less bias; selection of review procedures and anonymity practices can affect the degree of social-bias influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral to fellows/experts with particular expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial committee could refer submissions to fellows with particular expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, referral to named fellows with relevant expertise served as an early form of vetting; referrals were integral because papers often needed endorsement or referral to be considered at all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal written referee reports prior to acceptance ('written report of fitness')
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'written report of fitness' of submissions by one or more fellows was to be made before acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutionalized by 1832 at the Royal Society and similar to procedures introduced elsewhere; this formalization established a documentary basis for editorial decisions and acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish clear editorial standards and governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Early editorial management lacked 'any clear set of standards'; the Society later took financial and editorial control—by committee—to remedy problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The move to committee control and standardized procedures was driven by crises of credibility and aimed to create consistent standards for publication decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use peer review to guard against cronyism and elitism
rubrics_metrics.description: Refereeing was made standard (e.g., Nature in 1973) 'to raise the journal above accusations of cronyism and elitism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One explicit institutional purpose of formal refereeing was to demonstrate impartiality and distance editorial decisions from accusations of favoritism, which helped drive widespread adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limits of editorial responsibility (editorial disclaimers)
rubrics_metrics.description: From 1752 to 1957 the Transactions included an 'Advertisement' noting the Society could not 'answer for the certainty of the facts, or propriety of the reasonings' of papers; responsibility 'must still rest on the credit or judgement of their respective authors.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical practice included explicit disclaimers that peer review/refereeing did not guarantee correctness—an important caution about the role and limits of review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review as a credentialing mechanism for reputation and careers
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is 'crucial to building the reputation both of individual scientists and of the scientific enterprise at large' and 'reputations and careers are now expected to be built on peer-reviewed publication.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes the social function of peer review: beyond quality-control rhetoric, peer-reviewed publication serves as a currency for professional reputation and career advancement, which shapes incentives and practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review partly serves institutional goals (disarm attacks, protect finances, award prestige)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Refereeing and associated editorial practices' were intended to 'disarm specific attacks upon the eighteenth-century Society; sometimes, to protect the Society’s finances; and, by the later nineteenth century, to award prestige to members.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats peer review as an institutional tool used to build and protect the society/journal rather than solely a technical quality-control process; recognizes political and financial motivations behind procedural choices.
